title: SYSK Selects: How Igloos Work
summary: A Stuff You Should Know Selects rerun, introduced by Chuck as a curated pick, about how igloos work. The hosts trace shelter technology from clothing to enclosed snow houses, explain that "igloo" is an Inuit word meaning snow house, and discuss Inuit and Eskimo terminology, Inuit family and hunting life, and the claim of "kayak angst." They note igloos were mainly hunting shelters rather than permanent homes, describe how body heat and the snow's insulation keep the interior warm, and give a step-by-step overview of building one: cutting hard-packed snow blocks, spiraling them into a domed shape, setting a keystone block, sealing cracks, adding an entryway, and drilling air holes for ventilation. The episode closes with a listener mail item about a donation of six thousand LifeStraws and a sign-off directing listeners to HowStuffWorks for an illustrated igloo guide.

segments.title: Selects intro and Chuck's sick week
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Selects episode on igloos and the hosts banter about Chuck being under the weather after recording the Fainting Goats episode.

segments.title: Clothing, shelter, and the origins of igloos
segments.summary: The hosts frame clothing and shelter as early human technology, note that humans migrated into colder climates, and say enclosed snow shelters grew out of that line of development. They mention the Inuit word for snow house.

segments.title: Inuit and Eskimo names and people
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Inuit and Eskimo refer to the same people, who live across roughly 3,500 miles from Siberia to Alaska, Canada and Greenland. They discuss the origin of the term Eskimo, that Inuit is preferred, and Inuit family and hunting-centered society.

segments.title: Kayak angst and Inuit population
segments.summary: The hosts describe kayak angst, a fear of returning to kayak hunting after drifting at sea, which they present as specific to the Inuit. They also cite a Canadian Heritage figure of about 68,400 Inuit in Canada and say the group is thriving.

segments.title: Igloos as hunting shelters and Eskimo kisses
segments.summary: The hosts say Inuit did not live in igloos permanently; they were hunting shelters. They also explain the traditional Eskimo kiss as nose-to-face inhaling and correct the popular version.

segments.title: Why igloos stay warm
segments.summary: The hosts explain that igloos can be much warmer than outside air because body heat and wind chill reduction help, and that snow insulates. They also discuss how melting and refreezing strengthens the structure.

segments.title: How to build an igloo
segments.summary: The hosts outline the building process: finding hard-packed snow, cutting blocks with a snow saw, laying a circular foundation and spiraling up with a slanted, domed shape, using temporary sticks, setting a keystone block in the top hole, and sealing cracks with loose snow. They note a cut-out door and an L-shaped entryway help block wind.

segments.title: Ventilation and safety
segments.summary: The hosts stress drilling air holes so occupants do not suffocate, especially if using a camp stove or lantern. They reference a how-to article that is not a comprehensive guide.

segments.title: Igloos at ski resorts and Alex's igloo
segments.summary: The hosts note that igloos are used at ski resorts as overnight rentals and recall a cousin-in-law's large igloo built in Ohio.

segments.title: Chili Willie and igloo accuracy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the cartoon penguin Chili Willie and his igloo, which they say is accurate in shape though the setting is not.

segments.title: LifeStraw donation listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts recall a LifeStraw episode and say listener Steven Neeman's company, Eleventh Hour Search, will donate at least six thousand LifeStraws this year. They offer a T-shirt for listeners who save the world.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts direct listeners to HowStuffWorks for an illustrated igloo-building guide and to their social media and email for contact.
